L6: # Clinical Study for Cats with Mammary Cancer - Information for referring veterinarians
L7: 
L8: ##
L9: ## Why refer your patients?
L10: 
L11:   * The therapy (GCN2-IN-6) has been carefully tested in preclinical studies and is well-tolerated.
L12:   * Your referred patients will receive standard surgical care plus the investigational therapy.
L13:   * Participation contributes valuable data for advancing cancer treatments in both cats and humans.
L14: ## Study design highlights
L15: 
L16:   * Neo-adjuvant and adjuvant therapy administered around the time of mastectomy.
L17: 
L18:   * Safety and efficacy are continuously monitored.
L19: 
L20:   * Feline mammary adenocarcinoma is a validated model for TNBC research.
L21: ## Referral process
L22: 
L23:   * Eligible cats: cats diagnosed with mammary tumors, eligible for surgery.
L24: 
L25:   * As referring veterinarians, you can retain primary responsibility for routine care; the study team coordinates treatment administration and follow-up.
L26: 
L27:   * Participation is voluntary, and owners can withdraw at any time.
L28: ## Impact:
L29: 
L30: By referring cats to this study, you are helping advance cutting-edge cancer research, improve therapeutic options, and potentially enhance outcomes for both feline and human patients.
L31: ## Contact
L32: 
L33: Further information can be obtained by mailing Ada Krupa (adriana.krupa@ugent.be) or Hilde de Rooster (hilde.derooster@ugent.be) or by phone (+32 9 264 77 00).

L2: New Patients Welcome: OVC Researchers Evaluating Non-Surgical Treatment for Cats with Oral Cancer | University of Guelph
L3: 
L4: 【0†Image: A close-up of a brown and white tabby cat looking at the camera】
L5: # New Patients Welcome: OVC Researchers Evaluating Non-Surgical Treatment for Cats with Oral Cancer
L6: 
L7: Posted on Wednesday, August 28, 2024
L8: Researchers at the Ontario Veterinary College (OVC) are seeking feline patients to participate in a study exploring a minimally invasive treatment for oral cancer. Led by Dr. Michelle Oblak, Animal Health Partners Research Chair in Veterinary Medical Innovation, the research team is evaluating the use of nanoparticles and laser light therapy as a non-surgical treatment approach for cats diagnosed with oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma (OCSCC).
L9: ## About OCSCC
L10: 
L11: OCSCC is a relatively common and aggressive type of oral cancer in cats. It typically originates in the tissues of the mouth, including the gums, tongue and palate and presents as an ulcerative lesion that can cause drooling, bad breath and difficulty eating.
L12: OCSCC often progresses rapidly, invading surrounding tissues and bone within the oral cavity. Although rare, the disease may also spread to lymph nodes and organs. While the exact cause is not fully understood, factors such as chronic inflammation, exposure to carcinogens and viral infections (such as papillomavirus) may contribute to its development.
L13: ## Poor Treatment Prognosis
L14: 
L15: Early detection is an important factor in optimizing treatment outcomes for cats with OCSCC. Treatment approaches vary depending on the tumour size and location, and whether or not the cancer has spread.
L16: 
L17: Sadly, even with treatment, the prognosis for most cats is poor: cats treated with surgery, chemotherapy or radiation typically live for only one to four months. Less than 10 per cent of cats survive for one year after diagnosis.
L18: In most cases, treatment is aimed at managing the primary tumour and potential metastasis, as well as providing pain management.
L19: ## A New Treatment Approach
L20: 
L21: 【1†Image: Several images of an oral tumour on a cat. The tumour appears to be glowing because it has been injected with nanoparticles.†api.liveugconthub.uoguelph.dev】An oral tumour appears to glow following the injectionof Porphysomes during treatment of a feline patient at OVC
L22: Dr. Michelle Oblak is a veterinary surgical oncologist and professor in OVC’s Department of Clinical Studies. She is a recognized leader in translational research that explores novel approaches to cancer staging and treatment, including lymph node mapping, image-guided therapeutics and the use of 3D printing for surgical planning and reconstruction.
L23: 
L24: In this study, Oblak’s team combines light-activated nanoparticles (called Porphysomes) and photodynamic therapy (PDT) to target and destroy tumours.
L25: “We start by injecting Porphysomes into the patient’s bloodstream,” explains Oblak. “These nanoparticles preferentially accumulate in cancerous tissues. Using a specialized camera and light system, we can make them glow in the dark to quickly visualize the tumour, its margins and where the cancer has spread.”
L26: An added benefit of Porphysomes is that they make tissue more vulnerable to damage from laser light. The team uses an optical fiber to deliver a precise beam of laser light to the affected tissue, which activates the Porphysomes and induces tumour cell death without harming healthy surrounding tissues. This treatment may also potentially help in controlling the spread of the tumour.
L27: 【2†Image: Three people standing together and smiling at the camera outside in front of green trees†api.liveugconthub.uoguelph.dev】The Porphysome study research team(L-R: Charly McKenna, Dr. Michelle Oblak, Bridget Bane)
L28: 
L29: Oblak says the combination of Porphysomes and PDT is a welcome alternative to surgery.
L30: “We know that surgery may not be the best option for cats with OCSCC. And adjuvant therapies like chemotherapy and radiation generally do nothing to improve the overall survival rate of OCSCC. This treatment gives us a less-invasive option that shortens recovery time and reduces side effects, scarring and nerve damage associated with surgery.”
L31: 
L32: PDT has been used previously at OVC in dogs with thyroid cancer, and Oblak’s team is currently testing the therapy in dogs with all types of oral tumours.
L33: ## Collaborative Research that Benefits Pets and People
L34: 
L35: 【3†Image: Doctors in an operating room looking at a computer screen that is displaying images of an oral tumour in a cat.†api.liveugconthub.uoguelph.dev】Researchers from OVC and UHN perform a treatmentprocedure on a feline patient

L0@P0: Clinical trial combining radiation and chemotherapy in
L1@P0: dogs with high-grade glioma:
L2@P0: Information on participating in the trial
L3@P0: Diagnosis “glioma” – what now?
L4@P0: Dogs diagnosed with a brain tumor can confront their owners with a variety of symptoms, ranging from
L5@P0: behavioral changes to epileptic seizures. It is often assumed that the tumor is a so-called glioma. This
L6@P0: tumor, which originates in the supporting cells of the brain, is also frequently diagnosed in humans.
L7@P0: Around 75% of affected dogs suffer from an aggressive form – high-grade glioma.
L8@P0: The standard treatment for gliomas in humans is multimodal and consists of surgical removal, radiation
L9@P0: therapy, and chemotherapy. In dogs, however, radiation therapy is the most common form of treatment.
L10@P0: Chemotherapy is still not widely used for brain tumors in dogs.
L11@P0: Based on recent results in humans with gliomas, combined therapy using radiation therapy and
L12@P0: chemotherapy with lomustine and temozolomide can significantly prolong survival without
L13@P0: compromising quality of life. Lomustine and temozolomide are already used to treat other types of
L14@P0: tumors in dogs, and the tolerability of both drugs in dogs has already been investigated. In this study,
L15@P0: we want to investigate whether we can also significantly improve survival time in dogs with high-grade
L16@P0: gliomas without compromising their quality of life.
L17@P0: The radiotherapy
L18@P0: Radiotherapy takes place in 10 short treatment sessions on weekdays. The irradiation under short
L19@P0: anesthesia takes only a few minutes. From drop-off to pick-up, it takes about one to one and a half
L20@P0: hours for the animal to be fully awake and back on its feet. Most animals are brought in daily, but they
L21@P0-1: are also welcome to stay in the hospital during this time. Normally, we do not expect any side effects during and shortly after radiation therapy. The treatment itself is not painful, and patients live a normal
L22@P1: life alongside their daily sessions. There is a small residual risk of so-called late effects of radiation
L23@P1: therapy. We rarely see these, as we are able to minimize the risk through careful therapy planning and
L24@P1: thanks to very precise radiation equipment.
L25@P1: The chemotherapy
L26@P1: For the purposes of our study, all participating dogs will be randomly divided into two groups. Both
L27@P1: groups will receive radiation therapy, which is the current standard treatment. However, half of the dogs
L28@P1: will receive chemotherapy with temozolomide and lomustine. The other half will receive a placebo.
L29@P1: Throughout the study, neither the owners nor the treating veterinarians will know which group each dog
L30@P1: belongs to. At each visit, the dogs will undergo a clinical examination and a blood test before receiving
L31@P1: chemotherapy or the placebo. The medication will be administered in capsule form. This can be done
L32@P1: either at home or by us at the hospital.
L33@P1: Advantages and disadvantages of participating in the study, safety measures
L34@P1: Dogs that are suitable for participation in our study have undergone thorough clinical and neurological
L35@P1: examinations. A comprehensive blood test confirms that there are no other serious illnesses. An MRI
L36@P1: scan of the brain allows us to make a tentative diagnosis of high-grade glioma. For the purposes of the
L37@P1: study, it is necessary to confirm this suspected diagnosis with a minimally invasive tumor biopsy before
L38@P1: starting treatment. Before starting any chemotherapy, your pet will be thoroughly examined again and
L39@P1: blood tests will be performed. The drugs will only be administered if the tests are normal.
L40@P1: Residues of the chemotherapy drug may be excreted in urine and feces for several days and may also
L41@P1: be found in other bodily fluids such as vomit or blood. When cleaning up urine, feces, and vomit, owners
L42@P1: should therefore wear gloves (during the chemotherapy period) and ensure that these do not come into
L43@P1: contact with children or pregnant women.
L44@P1: By participating in the study, you will be supporting our research and future patients, and you will benefit
L45@P1: from a reduced price for radiation therapy. The brain biopsy and the costs of chemotherapy, including
L46@P1: the associated laboratory tests, are free of charge for study participants.
L47@P1: Follow-up checks
L48@P1: If you participate in our study, we will need to carry out regular follow-up checks.
L49@P1: Clinical and lab diagnostic examinations Before and 10 days after each chemotherapy
L50@P1: session
L51@P1: Magnetic resonance imaging Every 6 months after the start of therapy, or earlier
L52@P1: if clinically indicated.
L53@P1: Contact:
L54@P1: Please do not hesitate to contact us if you have any questions about participating in the study,
L55@P1: chemotherapy and radiation treatment, or the procedure for individual patients.
L56@P1: Direct contact study Phone: +41 44 635 9595
L57@P1: Email: neurologie@vetclinics.uzh.ch
